source.title: SoK: Membership Inference is Harder Than Previously Thought

record.tranche_reason: The study compares optimizers and dropout settings using training and testing accuracy, a different experimental setup from the claim versions' cited studies. Its main outcome is membership-inference success, which does not itself measure the claim's generalization behavior.
record.gate_note: The study reports optimizer and regularization comparisons of target-model training/testing accuracy in Table 2, and describes dropout's effect on test accuracy. Its MIA success-rate results are not rows for these versions. The versions' other named settings and mechanisms are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study's own training/test accuracy comparisons test V4 and V6 in additional architecture/dataset settings, although its main question concerns membership inference. Table 2 and appendix Tables 5–9 directly measure optimizer and dropout effects on held-out performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate when restricted to the tested attacks and selected targets: the authors find comparable membership-inference robustness across common optimizers and regularizers, and relate attack success more closely to the generalization gap than to a particular regularizer or absolute test accuracy. They explicitly do not claim that generalization defeats every black-box membership attack.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares optimizer and regularization settings in an MIA evaluation and reports target training/testing accuracy; it does not reproduce the original studies' generalization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and optimizer/dropout settings vary; the paper says MIA success rates remain close to chance across tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Membership-inference accuracy remains near chance across many optimizer, regularizer, leakage-volume, and depth settings for the selected well-generalizable targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the tested confidence-vector attack pipelines, aggregate membership inference is difficult on targets with small training/test accuracy gaps.

record.problems: For optimizer and dropout comparisons, the paper reports one 100-epoch setting on CIFAR-10 in Table 2; no uncertainty is stated for those accuracy values. It says additional dataset results are in appendix figures, some of which are figure-only.

untested.parts: No paired random-label and natural-label training/generalization experiment.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison; the attacker MLP is a different task.

Hyperparameter search scope and matched tuning budgets are unspecified. Broader tuning, Adam-to-SGD switching, and word-level language modeling are not tested. No adaptive optimizer matches SGD's training performance on CIFAR-10, so that stronger contrast is not demonstrated there.
No training-set-size sweep or joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization measures.
No memorization-based example removal and retraining; the discussion of Feldman and Zhang is cited work.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source for these versions. Its statement of no significant optimizer difference concerns membership-inference accuracy, not target test accuracy. Repeated attack-subset sampling does not provide uncertainty for the target accuracy comparisons. Appendix Tables 5–9 contain substantial omitted evidence; their separate optimizer and zero-dropout baselines must be preserved. Tuning details being unreported are an untested qualification, not themselves evidence for limits_scope.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization are not compared.
Network width relative to interpolation is not varied.
Convolutional and fully connected architecture performance is not compared.
The study does not report hyperparameter tuning scope, language benchmarks, or optimizer switching and decoupled weight decay comparisons.
Batch size and epoch-budget effects are not compared.
The study does not test very small training sets or removal of dropout and weight decay together with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap are not measured.
Memorized-example removal and retraining are not tested.
